title: Köttsoppa
lead:
{{Short description|Meat and vegetable soup}}
[[File:Meat soup.JPG|thumb|{{lang|sv|Köttsoppa|i=no}} as eaten in [[Scandinavia]] (Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark).]]
[[File:Kjötsúpa.JPG|thumb|180px|Icelandic {{lang|is|kjötsúpa}}.]]
{{lang|sv|'''Köttsoppa'''|i=no}} ({{IPA|sv|ˈɕœ̂tːˌsɔpːa|lang|small=no}}; {{langx|fi|'''lihakeitto'''|links=no}} {{IPA|fi|ˈlihɑˌkei̯tːo|}}; {{small|both}} {{lit|meat soup}}) is a clear [[meat]] and [[root vegetable]] [[Vegetable soup|soup]] eaten in [[Swedish cuisine|Sweden]] and [[Finnish cuisine|Finland]]. The meat, and the bones supplying the [[broth]], is [[beef]] (frequently [[Chuck steak|chuck]]), or sometimes [[pork]], [[reindeer]] or [[moose]]. Vegetables commonly used include [[carrot]], [[potato]], [[celeriac]], [[parsnip]], [[turnip]] and [[rutabaga]]. [[Green peas]] and [[white cabbage]] is also common. [[Leek]], [[peppercorn]]s and [[bay leaves]] are often added for seasoning. Meat and vegetables are cut to roughly [[dice|die]]-sized bits and boiled soft. An [[Icelandic cuisine|Icelandic]] variety, called {{lang|is|íslensk kjötsúpa}}, typically has [[Lamb and mutton|lamb]] with potatoes, carrots and cabbage.<ref name="Icelandic kjötsúpa">{{Cite web |url=https://islensktlambakjot.is/ |title=Heima - Lambakjöt |trans-title=Home - Lamb |website=islensktlambakjot.is |access-date=16 February 2025 |language=is}}</ref>

{{lang|sv|[[Knäckebröd]]|i=no}} with aged cheese such as {{lang|sv|[[prästost]]|i=no}} or [[Svecia]] is a popular side. {{lang|sv|Köttsoppa|i=no}} is also sometimes eaten with {{lang|sv|klimp}} – simple [[dumpling]]s the size of [[ping pong ball]]s made of [[wheat]], [[milk]] and [[egg (food)|egg]].<ref>{{cite web |first=Stefan |last=Holmström |url= http://www.svensksmak.se/index.php?action=bloggar_info&id=30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100814150820/http://www.svensksmak.se/index.php?action=bloggar_info&id=30 |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 14, 2010
|title=Köttsoppa |language=sv |website=Stefans matskola |access-date=March 1, 2020}}</ref>
